--- title: "Lesson 16 · Distributed lag and distributed lag non-linear models" subtitle: "Part IV · Time, space and clustering" description: "Lagged effects and harvesting, distributed lag models, the cross-basis, exposure–lag–response surfaces, cumulative exposure–response curves, the minimum morbidity temperature, and attributable fractions." --- ::: {.meta-pills} [About 3.5 hours]{} [Before this: Lessons 11 and 15]{} [Threads: uncertainty · shrinkage · frequentist ↔ Bayesian]{} [ ]{.pm-label} ::: ::: {.objectives} By the end of this lesson you will be able to - explain why exposure effects can be spread over several days, and recognize harvesting; - fit a distributed lag model and explain why constraining the lag curve stabilizes it; - describe a DLNM as a cross-basis: a spline in exposure crossed with a spline in lag; - read an exposure–lag–response surface, its slices, and the cumulative exposure–response curve; - estimate the minimum morbidity temperature with its uncertainty, and heat- and cold-attributable fractions. ::: ::: {.why} **Why it matters.** Heat acts within a day or two; cold acts over a week or more; and part of a heat effect may be visits brought forward by a few days. A model that uses only the same day's temperature underestimates cold effects and can exaggerate heat. DLNMs are now the standard approach in temperature–health research, including in large multi-country studies. ::: ## 16.1 Lagged effects and the distributed lag model {#s1} A hot day can raise visits on the same day, the next day and the day after. A **distributed lag model** includes the exposure on each of the previous L days, each with its own coefficient. Here the exposure is "degrees above 20°C" (heat only). Unconstrained, the lag coefficients are noisy, because temperatures on neighboring days are highly correlated. **Constraining** the lag curve to a smooth shape stabilizes it. Watch for negative coefficients a few days after a hot spell: that is **harvesting**. ```{=html}
``` ::::: {.triad} :::: {.a} ::: {.lab} [A]{.k}Standard notation ::: $$\log\mu_t = \alpha + \sum_{\ell=0}^{L}\beta_\ell\, h_{t-\ell} + s(t) + \gamma^\top \mathrm{dow}_t, \qquad h_t = \max(0, T_t - 20)$$ $$\text{constrained: } \beta_\ell = \sum_k \theta_k\, c_k(\ell), \qquad \text{cumulative} = \sum_\ell \beta_\ell$$ :::: :::: {.b} ::: {.lab} [B]{.k}Model list and R ::: ```r cb <- dlnm::crossbasis(pmax(city_daily$temp - 20, 0), lag = 10, argvar = list(fun = "lin"), arglag = list(fun = "ns", df = 4)) fit <- glm(visits ~ cb + splines::ns(t, df = 35) + dow, family = quasipoisson, data = city_daily) ``` :::: :::: {.d} ::: {.lab} [D]{.k}How to read it ::: - $\beta_\ell$: the effect of heat on day $t-\ell$ on visits on day $t$: the lag-specific effect. - $h_{t-\ell}$: the heat exposure $\ell$ days earlier. - $h_t$: heat on day $t$: degrees above 20°C (0 below). - $L$: the maximum lag, here 21 days. - $\theta_k$: the coefficients of the lag basis: a few numbers that define the whole smooth lag curve. - $c_k(\ell)$: the lag basis functions: smooth curves over lags. - $\text{cumulative}$: the cumulative effect: the sum over all lags. :::: ::::: ::: {.further} **Further reading:** @schwartz2000distributed on distributed lag models and harvesting; @armstrong2006models on lagged temperature effects; @gasparrini2010distributed on constraining lag structures. ::: ## 16.2 The DLNM: an exposure–lag–response surface {#s2} Temperature effects are both **nonlinear** (a U shape) and **lagged**. A DLNM handles both at once with a **cross-basis**: a spline in temperature multiplied by a spline in lag. The result is a surface: the relative risk at every combination of temperature and lag, relative to a reference temperature. Read it through slices: pick a temperature to see how its effect unfolds over the following days, or pick a lag to see the exposure–response at that delay. ```{=html}
lower risk than at the referencehigher risk
``` ::::: {.triad} :::: {.a} ::: {.lab} [A]{.k}Standard notation ::: $$\log\mu_t = \alpha + \sum_{j}\sum_{k}\eta_{jk}\, w_{t,jk} + s(t) + \gamma^\top \mathrm{dow}_t$$ $$w_{t,jk} = \sum_{\ell=0}^{L} b_j(T_{t-\ell})\, c_k(\ell)$$ ::: {.note} $b_j$: spline basis in temperature; $c_k$: spline basis in lag; the $\eta_{jk}$ define the whole surface. ::: :::: :::: {.b} ::: {.lab} [B]{.k}Model list and R ::: ```r cb <- dlnm::crossbasis(city_daily$temp, lag = 21, argvar = list(fun = "ns", knots = quantile( city_daily$temp, c(.10, .50, .90))), arglag = list(fun = "ns", knots = dlnm::logknots(21, 3))) fit <- glm(visits ~ cb + splines::ns(t, df = 35) + dow, family = quasipoisson, data = city_daily) ``` :::: :::: {.d} ::: {.lab} [D]{.k}How to read it ::: - $\eta_{jk}$: the cross-basis coefficients: together they define the whole exposure–lag–response surface. - $w_{t,jk}$: the cross-basis variable: exposure history on day $t$ transformed by basis $j$ and weighted by lag basis $k$. - $b_j(T_{t-\ell})$: exposure basis function $j$ applied to the temperature $\ell$ days earlier. - $c_k(\ell)$: lag basis function $k$ at lag $\ell$. - $L$: the maximum lag. :::: ::::: ::: {.further} **Further reading:** @gasparrini2010distributed introduced DLNMs; @gasparrini2011distributed describe the dlnm package; @bhaskaran2013time place DLNMs in the time-series framework. ::: ## 16.3 The cumulative curve and the minimum morbidity temperature {#s3} Summing the surface over all lags gives the **cumulative exposure–response curve**: the total effect of a day's temperature over the following three weeks. Its lowest point is the **minimum morbidity temperature** (MMT), the usual reference. The MMT is itself an estimate, and often an uncertain one. Simulating from the fitted coefficients shows how uncertain, and what that uncertainty does to the relative risks reported against it. ```{=html}
``` ::::: {.triad} :::: {.a} ::: {.lab} [A]{.k}Standard notation ::: $$\log RR_{\text{cum}}(x) = \sum_{\ell=0}^{L}\sum_{j,k}\eta_{jk}\,\big[b_j(x) - b_j(x_{\text{ref}})\big]\, c_k(\ell)$$ $$\mathrm{MMT} = \arg\min_x \log RR_{\text{cum}}(x)$$ :::: :::: {.b} ::: {.lab} [B]{.k}Model list and R ::: ```r pred <- dlnm::crosspred(cb, fit, cen = 20, by = 0.1) mmt <- pred$predvar[which.min(pred$allRRfit)] pred2 <- dlnm::crosspred(cb, fit, cen = mmt, at = quantile(city_daily$temp, c(.01, .99))) pred2$allRRfit; pred2$allRRlow; pred2$allRRhigh ``` :::: :::: {.d} ::: {.lab} [D]{.k}How to read it ::: - $\log RR_{\text{cum}}(x)$: the cumulative log relative risk at temperature $x$, summed over lags. - $b_j(x)$: exposure basis function $j$ at temperature $x$. - $x_{\text{ref}}$: the reference temperature: RRs are relative to it. - $\mathrm{MMT}$: the minimum morbidity temperature: where the cumulative curve is lowest. - $\arg\min_x$: "the value of $x$ that minimizes". :::: :::: {.c} ::: {.lab} [C]{.k}How it's reported ::: [ ]{#cReport} :::: ::::: ::: {.callout-warning title="Common pitfall"} Reporting relative risks against the MMT as if the MMT were known. Conventional intervals shrink to zero width at the reference, hiding its uncertainty. Report an interval for the MMT itself, obtained by simulation or bootstrap. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon="false" title="R code (optional): a DLNM for daily visits"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} city_daily <- visits |> group_by(date) |> summarise(visits = sum(visits), temp = first(temp_city), dow = first(dow), .groups = "drop") |> mutate(t = row_number()) cb <- dlnm::crossbasis(city_daily$temp, lag = 21, argvar = list(fun = "ns", knots = quantile(city_daily$temp, c(.10, .50, .90))), arglag = list(fun = "ns", knots = dlnm::logknots(21, 3))) fit <- glm(visits ~ cb + splines::ns(t, df = 35) + dow, family = quasipoisson, data = city_daily) pred <- dlnm::crosspred(cb, fit, cen = 20, by = 0.1) mmt <- pred$predvar[which.min(pred$allRRfit)] pred <- dlnm::crosspred(cb, fit, cen = mmt, by = 0.1) plot(pred, "overall", xlab = "Temperature (°C)", ylab = "Cumulative RR (lags 0-21)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lesson-16_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){width=672} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} mmt ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] 19.4 ``` ::: ::: ::: **Two ways.** The MMT's uncertainty, simulated from the fitted coefficients (frequentist) or drawn from their posterior (Bayesian). With flat priors the two use the same draws; a prior that shrinks the cross-basis changes them. ```{=html}

``` ::: {.further} **Further reading:** @tobias2017investigating on estimating uncertainty in the minimum mortality temperature; @gasparrini2015mortality report cumulative temperature–mortality curves in 384 locations; @gasparrini2011distributed on predicting from a DLNM. ::: ## 16.4 Heat- and cold-attributable visits {#s4} From the cumulative curve, each day's visits can be split into those attributable to that day's temperature (relative to the MMT) and the rest. Summed over the period, this gives the **attributable fraction** for heat (days warmer than the MMT) and cold (days colder). Uncertainty is again obtained by simulating from the coefficients. ```{=html}
``` ::::: {.triad} :::: {.a} ::: {.lab} [A]{.k}Standard notation ::: $$AF_t = 1 - \exp\{-\log RR_{\text{cum}}(T_t)\}, \qquad AN = \sum_t y_t\, AF_t$$ $$AF_{\text{heat}} = \frac{\sum_{t: T_t > \mathrm{MMT}} y_t\, AF_t}{\sum_t y_t}$$ :::: :::: {.b} ::: {.lab} [B]{.k}Model list and R ::: ```r # attrdl() from the dlnm tutorial code # (Gasparrini & Leone 2014): # attrdl(city_daily$temp, cb, city_daily$visits, # fit, type = "af", cen = mmt, # range = c(mmt, 100), sim = TRUE) ``` :::: :::: {.d} ::: {.lab} [D]{.k}How to read it ::: - $AF_t$: the share of day $t$'s visits attributable to its temperature (relative to the MMT). - $y_t$: the visits on day $t$. - $AN$: the attributable number: summed over days. - $AF_{\text{heat}}$: the heat-attributable fraction: from days above the MMT only. Cold uses days below. - $\mathrm{MMT}$: the reference temperature separating heat from cold. :::: :::: {.c} ::: {.lab} [C]{.k}How it's reported ::: [ ]{#aReport} :::: ::::: ::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Bayesian preview"} A Bayesian DLNM gives the lag curve a smoothing prior instead of a fixed number of spline knots, and computes the MMT and attributable fractions on every posterior draw, so their uncertainty comes for free. Lesson 25 builds a district-level Bayesian DLNM in which each district's curve borrows strength from its neighbors. ::: ::: {.further} **Further reading:** @gasparrini2014attributable define attributable risk from distributed lag models; @gasparrini2015mortality apply it across countries; @rockhill1998use on interpreting attributable fractions. ::: ## Check your understanding {#quiz} ```{=html}
``` ## Key takeaways {#take} - Exposure effects can be delayed and spread over days. Heat acts quickly; cold acts over a week or more. - Unconstrained lag coefficients are unstable; constraining the lag curve with a spline stabilizes them. - A DLNM crosses a spline in exposure with a spline in lag, giving an exposure–lag–response surface. - The cumulative curve sums effects over lags; its minimum, the MMT, is the usual reference, and it is uncertain. - Attributable fractions for heat and cold follow from the cumulative curve, with uncertainty from simulation. ## Concepts at a glance {#concepts} Ideas from this lesson that are easily confused, side by side. | Concept | What it is | How it differs | |---|---|---| | **Lag** | The delay between exposure and outcome, in days. | Lag 0 is the same day; lag 3 is three days later. | | **Lag-specific effect** | The effect of exposure on one day on the outcome a given number of days later. | The cumulative effect sums lag-specific effects over all lags. | | **Cumulative effect** | The total effect of a sustained exposure over the whole lag period. | What burden calculations use; individual lags can be noisy or negative. | | **Distributed lag model (DLM)** | A model for the effect at each lag, constrained to be smooth over lags. | Assumes a linear exposure–response; a DLNM lets it be non-linear too. | | **DLNM** | A model whose effect varies smoothly over both exposure level and lag. | Built from a cross-basis; generalizes the DLM. | | **Cross-basis** | Every exposure basis function multiplied by every lag basis function. | Its coefficients describe a surface; neither basis alone does. | | **Exposure basis vs lag basis** | The spline over temperature vs the spline over lags. | Two separate choices of type, knots and df; the cross-basis combines them. | | **Knots in the exposure dimension** | Temperatures where the exposure spline's pieces join (e.g., percentiles). | Shape the exposure–response curve; lag knots shape the lag curve. | | **Knots in the lag dimension** | Lags where the lag spline's pieces join (often log-spaced: dense early, sparse late). | Shape how the effect spreads over days; unrelated to temperature values. | | **Spline vs natural spline** | A piecewise polynomial vs one constrained to be linear beyond the outer knots. | Natural splines behave better at extreme temperatures, where data are sparse. | | **Minimum morbidity temperature (MMT)** | The temperature with the lowest cumulative risk. | The usual reference for RRs and the heat/cold split; it has its own uncertainty. | | **Harvesting** | A deficit of events after a peak, as frail people's events were brought forward by a few days. | Shows as negative effects at later lags; ignored by single-lag models. | ```{=html}
